newsitem.title: IRAQ: FEATURE-In Iraq, Ramadan sweets galore after oil-for-food deal.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-In Iraq, Ramadan sweets galore after oil-for-food deal.

text.p: Baghdad confectioneries are again brimming with sticky sweets made especially for the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, thanks to Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

On every street corner, sweets shops display large plates full of domestic delights such as baqlawa, a sugary roll stuffed with walnuts or almonds, and zalabiya, floury spirals dipped in boiling sugar syrup.
"Six Ramadans have passed and we could not find any baqlawa in the market. Now it is plentiful wherever you go in Baghdad," said shopper Um Ashour, holding three packs of the sweets.

Such delicacies had been hard to find since the government banned the making and sale of food items using sugar after the United Nations imposed sweeping economic sanctions on Iraq for invading Kuwait in 1990.

But Baghdad scrapped the ban on sweets when it started exporting oil in December under the U.N. deal that allows it to sell oil worth $2 billion over six months and use most of the proceeds to buy food and medicine -- although by late January the first such food imports had yet to arrive.
SWEETS STILL TOO EXPENSIVE FOR MANY

The price of a kg (2.2 lb) of sugar, meanwhile, has soared by nearly 50 percent since early December to 650 dinars ($0.55). Many attribute the rise, and a substantial increase in the price of flour, to the lifting of the ban on sugar consumption.
For many, Ramadan sweets, essential for fast-breaking "iftar" meal, are beyond reach. A kg of baqlawa costs about 3,500 dinars -- almost a month's salary of a civil servant.
"If we have lentil soup we are lucky. Baqlawa and zalabiya are still a luxury for us," said Kauthar Jameel.

Every evening Kauthar sends the oldest of her six children, Samia, to the nearest mosque to pick up alms -- mostly stewed rice, dates and soup -- which rich Baghdadis donate during Ramadan. The holy month started on Januray 10.
Under the government rationing system, each Iraqi is entitled to half a kg (1.1 lb) of sugar a month at giveaway prices. This covers less than one-third of their needs.
But the government says that once the supplies bought under the oil-for-food deal start arriving, the monthly ration will be raised to two kg (4.4 lb).
"This has encouraged the government to remove the ban on sugar consumption and what you see is a flood of Iraqi-made sweets," said one Baghdad trader.
SWEETS SHOPS ADVERTISE ON TV
Advertisements of local sweets have swept the Shebab television, a popular channel owned by President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday.

In Karrada, one of Baghdad's main thoroughfares, street vendors spread all kinds of local and foreign sweets on the sidewalk. Iraqi-made colas sold in Pepsi-Cola bottles, banned for the past six years, compete with foreign brands.

"I have lost millions of dinars since the government ordered the ban on sugar-related foods. I am back again after a long wait but still keep my fingers crossed," said the owner of a sweets shop in al-Mansour district, one of Baghdad's wealthiest.
Iraqis used to consume huge amounts of sugar in pre-sanction times -- more than 750,000 tonnes a year.
Under the partial oil sales deal Iraq will need to import 255,500 tonnes of sugar in six months to be able to hand out two kg to each of its more than 20 million people.
Some $115 million has been allocated to sugar purchases in the first six months of the renewable deal.
